chapter.name: Citizenship: Rights and Duties
chapter.blurb: What it means to be a citizen of India in law and in everyday life: the six broad categories of Fundamental Rights with the article ranges Fig. 5.2 attaches to them, the eleven Fundamental Duties of Article 51A, the difference between equality, equity and inclusion, and how discrimination -- open or hidden -- blocks people from rights the Constitution has already given them.

concepts.name: Who is a citizen: legal identity and social responsibility
concepts.description: What the chapter means by a citizen, how a citizen differs from a resident, the rights and duties citizenship carries, and the four concepts -- rights, duties, discrimination and inclusion -- that the chapter sets out to explore.
concepts.idea: Citizenship is not only a stamp on a document; it is also something a person does in everyday life.
concepts.rule: A citizen is someone who legally belongs to a country and is a member of its political community, that is, they can take part in the decision-making of the country. In a democracy citizenship gives rights such as voting, free speech, and living and working safely, but these rights have limits. At the same time citizens have duties like obeying the law, paying taxes, respecting others, and helping keep society safe. Citizenship is therefore both a legal identity and a social responsibility: as a legal identity it formally connects people to their country, and as a social responsibility it creates a sense of belonging and unites people through shared values, rights and duties. Living in a place makes a person a resident, but citizenship is a formal, legal membership in a country, so not every resident of a country is a citizen, and a citizen can even reside in another country. Citizenship is about active participation -- paying taxes, helping others in need, protecting the environment -- and it also grants the power to question unfair practices and stand up for what is right. In India all citizens are equal under the Constitution despite differences of language, religion or culture, and the Citizenship Act of 1955 and the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of 2019 set the rules for gaining or losing citizenship. The chapter focuses on four concepts: rights, duties, discrimination and inclusion; the first three are specifically mentioned in the Constitution, while inclusion is an affirmative way to ensure non-discrimination.
concepts.example: Kruti, a new student, was teased on the playground for her accent. Sonali and Harshada told the bullies to stop, and then invited Kruti to join their badminton team so she would feel welcome. They showed what it means to be good citizens: they stood up for someone who needed help and made sure everyone felt included.

questions.a: Sample: The chapter states that in India all citizens are equal under the Constitution despite differences of language, religion or culture, so a difference of language takes nothing away from a person's standing. Citizenship is a formal, legal membership in the country, not a matter of which neighbourhood someone grew up in, and even if the family were residents rather than citizens the chapter's idea of inclusion means ensuring no one is left out because of language. Citizenship as a social responsibility asks the neighbours to do the opposite of what they are doing: to create a sense of belonging, as Sonali and Harshada did for Kruti when she was teased for her accent.
s: Cites that all citizens are equal under the Constitution despite differences of language, religion or culture

questions.q: The chapter tells the story of Kruti and the badminton team before it gives any definition of a citizen. Why might the writers have arranged it in that order?
questions.a: Sample: The story shows citizenship as something done rather than something possessed, which is the chapter's main claim. Sonali and Harshada hold no office and pass no law; they simply stop the teasing and then include Kruti, and the chapter calls that being good citizens. Putting the story first means that when the legal definition arrives -- a member of the political community who can take part in decision-making -- the reader already understands that the legal identity is only one half, and that the social responsibility half is visible in an ordinary playground. A definition given first would have made citizenship sound like a document.
s: Explains that the story presents citizenship as active conduct rather than a status
Notes that it prepares the reader for the two-sided definition, legal identity and social responsibility
Draws out the effect on the reader, for example that a definition alone would make citizenship seem merely a document

questions.q: At the festival, four problems arose: Meena, Ravi, the children kept busy cleaning, and Gaganjit. State the ground of exclusion in each case, and then say what all four have in common.
questions.a: Sample: Meena was excluded on the ground of gender, being told girls should not speak on stage. Ravi was excluded on the ground of economic or social background, as a street vendor's son turned away while a wealthy boy was welcomed. The children kept busy cleaning were excluded from education, being made to work instead of going to school. Gaganjit was excluded on the ground of disability, because the exhibition hall had no ramp. What all four share is that none of them was kept out for anything they had done or failed to do: each was shut out by an identity or a circumstance, and in each case a fundamental right -- to equality, to education, to dignity -- was being denied. All four were also fixed by people noticing and acting, not by the children changing themselves.
s: Names the ground correctly for at least three of the four cases
Identifies the common thread that each was excluded by identity or circumstance, not by conduct
Adds that a fundamental right was denied in each, or that each was fixed by others speaking up

questions.q: 'A person who obeys the law and pays her taxes has done everything that citizenship asks of her.' Do you agree? Judge this using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: Only partly. Obeying the law and paying taxes are both listed by the chapter as duties of a citizen, so such a person has met a real part of what citizenship asks. But the chapter describes citizenship as active participation, which also includes helping others in need and protecting the environment, and it gives citizens the power to question unfair practices and stand up for what is right. By that standard a person who quietly obeys but never speaks when someone is treated unfairly has left out the part of citizenship the chapter cares most about -- the part Sonali and Harshada showed. So the statement names a necessary part of citizenship but mistakes it for the whole.
s: Concedes that obeying the law and paying taxes are genuine duties named by the chapter
Argues that the chapter also requires active participation, helping others and questioning unfair practices
Reaches a clear judgement that the statement is incomplete rather than simply wrong

Fourth, check that every hall on the route has a ramp and a step-free path, because Gaganjit could not enter the exhibition hall in his wheelchair. Each check turns last year's complaint into something the team confirms before the festival starts, rather than something a child has to protest about during it.

Gives a check addressing exclusion by economic background, with the reason drawn from Ravi's case
Gives a check addressing children working instead of attending school
Gives a check addressing physical access for a wheelchair user, with the reason drawn from Gaganjit's case

concepts.name: What rights are, the six Fundamental Rights, and how they are enforced
concepts.description: Rights as justified claims rather than wishes, the six broad categories of Fundamental Rights that Fig. 5.2 names with their article ranges, and the right to constitutional remedies that makes the rest enforceable.
concepts.idea: A right is a claim that can be justified and, in India, one that a court can be asked to protect.
concepts.rule: Rights are what we are all entitled to as human beings and members of society, but not everything we want can be called a right. Rights are what we need to live with dignity, safety and respect, such as the right to education, to earn a living, or to express our ideas; actions that cause harm to ourselves or to others cannot be considered rights. True rights are those that support the wellbeing and dignity of all, and so rights are justified claims. The Constitution gives Fundamental Rights, the basic rights every Indian citizen has, and lists six broad categories of them: the right to equality (Articles 14-18), the right to freedom (Articles 19-22), the right against exploitation (Articles 23 and 24), the right to freedom of religion (Articles 25-28), cultural and educational rights (Articles 29 and 30), and the right to constitutional remedies (Article 32). These rights can be enforced by law, which means that if they are violated people can approach the courts for justice. They protect people both from unfair treatment by others and from unfair actions by the government, so that every person is treated fairly and power is not misused. The right to constitutional remedies allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court if their fundamental rights are violated, and it ensures that these rights are not just promises on paper but can actually be protected and enforced.
concepts.example: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said during the Constituent Assembly Debates that if he were asked to name the most important article in the Constitution, an article without which the Constitution would be a nullity, he could refer to no other than the right to constitutional remedies: it is, he said, the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.

questions.a: It means a right is not simply anything a person demands: the claim has to be one that can be defended. The chapter's test is that rights are what we need in order to live with dignity, safety and respect, such as education, a living or the expression of our ideas, and that anything which harms oneself or others cannot qualify. A claim is justified when granting it supports the wellbeing and dignity of all.

The other fundamental rights state what a citizen is entitled to, but without a way of enforcing them they would remain promises on paper. The right to constitutional remedies lets a citizen go to the Supreme Court when a right is violated, so Ambedkar said that without this article the Constitution would be a nullity.

Article 29, protection of language, script and cultural rights

questions.q: A citizen believes a government order has taken away one of her fundamental rights. Using the chapter, state what she can do and which right makes that possible.
questions.a: She can approach the courts for justice, and in particular she may go to the Supreme Court. This is possible because of the right to constitutional remedies, listed as Article 32, which exists precisely so that fundamental rights can be protected and enforced rather than remaining promises on paper. The chapter also notes that fundamental rights protect people from unfair actions by the government, not only from unfair treatment by other people.
s: States that she can approach the courts, or the Supreme Court, for justice
Names the right to constitutional remedies as what makes this possible

questions.q: An eight-year-old child is found working in a factory. Using the table on page 154 and Fig. 5.2, state the article that bans this, the broad category of Fundamental Rights it belongs to, and what can be done if the ban is ignored.
questions.a: Articles 23 and 24 ban human trafficking, forced labour and child labour, so those are the articles involved. They fall under the broad category called the right against exploitation. If the ban is ignored, the matter can be taken to the courts, because fundamental rights can be enforced by law; the chapter also describes the Childline 1098 helpline being used in exactly such a case.
s: Names Article 23 and 24, or the ban on child and forced labour
Names the right against exploitation as the category
States that the courts can be approached, or names Childline 1098 as a route

questions.q: A younger cousin reads the list of six Fundamental Rights and asks why one of them is only about going to court. Explain to him why that right belongs on the list at all.
questions.a: Sample: The other five say what a citizen is entitled to -- equality, freedom, protection from exploitation, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights. But a statement of entitlement does nothing on its own if no one can be made to honour it. The right to constitutional remedies is the one that lets a citizen take a violation to the Supreme Court, so it is what turns the other five from promises on paper into things that can actually be protected and enforced. That is why Ambedkar called it the soul and the heart of the Constitution and said that without it the Constitution would be a nullity. It is on the list because it is the right that guards all the other rights.
s: Distinguishes the five rights that state entitlements from the one that enforces them
Explains that without enforcement the other rights would be promises on paper
Supports the point with Ambedkar's judgement or with the route to the Supreme Court

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fundamental Rights in India are more than statements of good intention. Reason (R): They can be enforced by law, so a person whose right is violated may approach the courts for justice. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: 'Not everything we want can be called a right.' Analyse the test the chapter offers for telling a right apart from a mere want.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter's test has two halves. The first is a test of need: rights are what we need to live with dignity, safety and respect, and its examples -- education, earning a living, expressing our ideas -- are all things without which a person cannot grow, learn and live freely. The second is a test of harm: actions that cause harm to ourselves or to others cannot be considered rights, however strongly they are wanted. Putting the halves together, the chapter says true rights are those that support the wellbeing and dignity of all, which is why it calls them justified claims. The test is therefore not about how badly something is wanted but about whether the claim can be defended for everyone at once.
s: Identifies the need half of the test: what is required to live with dignity, safety and respect
Identifies the harm half: what harms oneself or others cannot be a right
Draws the two together into the idea of a justified claim that supports the wellbeing of all

questions.q: Page 154 prints a table of articles and adds, 'You need not memorise these, but as a citizen of India, you should be aware of them.' Analyse why both halves of that sentence matter.
questions.a: Sample: The first half protects the reader from mistaking the subject for a list to be learnt by heart. What matters about Article 17 is that untouchability is abolished, not the number; a student who memorises numbers but cannot recognise an injustice has learnt nothing useful. The second half protects against the opposite error, of treating rights as vague good feelings. Knowing that a guarantee exists in a specific place in the Constitution is what lets a citizen say that a particular act is not merely unkind but unlawful, and gives them something definite to take to a court. Together the two halves say that awareness, not recall, is the aim, which matches the chapter's own line that these articles help us understand how the Constitution and the Judiciary protect the dignity and equality of every citizen.
s: Explains what the 'need not memorise' half guards against, that is treating rights as numbers to be recalled
Explains what the 'should be aware' half secures, that is definite, citable guarantees rather than vague feelings
Reaches a conclusion about awareness rather than recall being the aim

questions.q: 'Fundamental Rights exist to protect citizens from each other; they have nothing to say about the government.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim is wrong, and the chapter says so directly on page 148: fundamental rights protect people from unfair treatment by others and also protect people from unfair actions by the government, so that power is not misused. The half the claim gets right is that citizens can indeed wrong each other, and rights speak to that too. But several of the rights are aimed squarely at the state: the right to equality prevents the government from giving out special titles and requires equal opportunity in public employment, and the right to constitutional remedies exists so that a citizen can take the government itself to court. A right that could not be used against the government would be of little use to the person it is meant to protect, so the claim must be rejected.
s: Rejects the claim and cites the chapter's statement that rights protect against unfair actions by the government
Supports it with an example such as equal opportunity in public employment, titles, or going to court against the state
Concedes the partial truth that rights also govern conduct between citizens, and still reaches a clear verdict

questions.q: Design a short 'Know Your Rights' card for your school notice board. Give it a heading, list the six broad categories of Fundamental Rights, add one line saying what makes them enforceable, and add one line warning against a common misunderstanding.
questions.a: Sample: Heading -- Know Your Rights: the six Fundamental Rights of every Indian citizen. The list: the right to equality; the right to freedom; the right against exploitation; the right to freedom of religion; cultural and educational rights; and the right to constitutional remedies. What makes them enforceable: these are not promises on paper, because a person whose fundamental right is violated can approach the courts, and the right to constitutional remedies allows a citizen to go to the Supreme Court. The warning: not everything you want is a right -- a right is a justified claim, needed to live with dignity, safety and respect, and anything that harms you or others cannot be one.
s: Gives a suitable heading for a notice-board card
Lists all six broad categories correctly
States what makes the rights enforceable, referring to the courts or to constitutional remedies
Warns against a real misunderstanding, such as treating every want as a right

concepts.name: The right to equality, and equality versus equity
concepts.description: What the right to equality guarantees -- equality before the law, equal opportunity, an end to untouchability and a bar on special titles -- and the distinction Fig. 5.3 draws between giving everyone the same support and giving everyone the support they need.
concepts.idea: Giving everybody exactly the same thing is not the same as being fair to everybody.
concepts.rule: The right to equality ensures that every person is treated equally before the law, has equal opportunities in jobs and education, and cannot be discriminated against because of religion, race, caste, gender or place of birth. It also ends practices like untouchability and prevents the government from giving out special titles to individuals, except for military or academic honours. Alongside this the chapter draws a distinction: equality means everyone receives the exact same support, while equity means everyone gets the support they need, fairly. Providing the same thing to every individual does not always provide the same benefit, because of differences among people, and those differences may be due to inequality and discrimination which may have been carried historically too. Equity is defined in the chapter as the quality of being fair and just, especially in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities. Many initiatives by the government and by civil society organisations aim to establish equity in such cases.
concepts.example: The Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign was meant to build awareness in society and also to provide support to girls' education -- an example of equity, because it directs extra support towards a group that had been held back, rather than offering the same thing to everyone.

questions.a: Untouchability
o: Untouchability
Bonded labour
Human trafficking
Child marriage

questions.a: Military or academic honours

questions.q: In Fig. 5.3 the panel headed EQUITY is explained with the line, 'Everyone gets the ____ they need, fairly.'

questions.a: Physical appearance

questions.a: Equality gives everyone the exact same support, while equity gives everyone the support they need
o: Equality gives everyone the exact same support, while equity gives everyone the support they need
Equality applies to adults, while equity applies only to children
Equality is written in the Constitution, while equity is against the law
Equality is about money, while equity is about education

questions.q: Why does the chapter say that providing the same thing to every individual does not always provide the same benefit?
questions.a: Because of differences among people, which may be due to inequality and discrimination carried historically
o: Because of differences among people, which may be due to inequality and discrimination carried historically
Because the government never has enough resources for everyone
Because some people refuse the support that is offered to them
Because benefits are always shared out by lottery

questions.q: Give the chapter's definition of equity, and explain in one sentence how it differs from equality.
questions.a: The chapter defines equity as the quality of being fair and just, especially in a way that takes account of and seeks to address existing inequalities. It differs from equality in that equality hands everyone the exact same support, while equity looks first at what each person actually needs, so that the support given produces a fair result rather than merely an identical one.
s: Gives the definition of equity as being fair and just while addressing existing inequalities
Contrasts it with equality as the same support for everyone

questions.q: Consider these statements. (I) The right to equality allows the government to give special titles to any individual it wishes. (II) The right to equality guarantees equal opportunities in jobs and education. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II
o: Only II
Only I
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: What was the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign meant to do, and why does the chapter offer it as an example of equity rather than of equality?
questions.a: It was meant to build awareness in society and to provide support to girls' education. It is an example of equity because it does not hand the same thing to every child; it directs extra support towards girls, a group whose education had been held back by inequality carried from the past. Equity means taking account of that existing inequality and addressing it, which is exactly what the campaign sets out to do.
s: States the campaign's two aims: building awareness and supporting girls' education
Explains that it targets extra support at a group held back, which is equity rather than identical treatment

questions.q: A class is given one printed textbook each, but one student is blind and cannot read print. Applying the chapter's principle of equity, the school should
questions.a: Provide her the book in a form she can read, such as braille
o: Provide her the book in a form she can read, such as braille
Give every student in the class a second printed copy
Give her the same printed book and ask a friend to read it aloud after school
Withdraw the printed books from everyone so that no one has an advantage

questions.q: In the left-hand panel of Fig. 5.3 each of the three people is given a box of the same size. Describe what happens, and explain why the right-hand panel is the fairer arrangement.
questions.a: In the left panel everyone receives the exact same support, so the tallest person can see over the fence easily while the shortest still cannot see at all: identical boxes do not produce identical benefit, because the three people did not start from the same height. In the right panel the boxes are shared out according to need, so all three can see over the fence. That is equity -- everyone gets the support they need, fairly -- and it is fairer because it looks at the result rather than only at the handout.
s: Describes that identical boxes leave the shortest person still unable to see
Explains that the right panel shares support by need so that all three can see, which is equity

questions.q: A government announces a grand new title to be conferred on a wealthy businessman for donating to a public fund. Which part of the right to equality does this run against?
questions.a: The bar on the government giving out special titles to individuals
o: The bar on the government giving out special titles to individuals
The guarantee of equality before the law
The guarantee of equal opportunity in jobs and education
The ending of the practice of untouchability

questions.q: A hostel refuses admission to a boy because of the village he was born in. Name the ground of discrimination involved and the right that is violated.
questions.a: The ground is place of birth, which page 148 lists among the grounds on which the right to equality says no one may be discriminated against, alongside religion, race, caste and gender. The right violated is therefore the right to equality, one of the six Fundamental Rights, and the boy or his family may approach the courts because fundamental rights can be enforced by law.
s: Names place of birth as the ground
Names the right to equality as the right violated

questions.q: A school has money for scholarships and is choosing between two plans. Plan A gives every student the same amount. Plan B gives a larger amount to students whose families cannot afford the fees. Say which plan is equality and which is equity, state which one the chapter's reasoning supports, and give the reason.
questions.a: Plan A is equality, because everyone receives the exact same support. Plan B is equity, because the support is shared out according to what each student needs. The chapter's reasoning supports Plan B, since it says that providing the same thing to every individual does not provide the same benefit on account of differences among them, differences that may be due to inequality carried historically. Under Plan A a family that can already pay the fees gains a bonus while a family that cannot pay is still short, so the same handout leaves the original gap untouched.
s: Identifies Plan A as equality and Plan B as equity
States that the chapter's reasoning supports Plan B
Gives the reason: identical support does not give identical benefit and leaves the existing gap in place

questions.q: A classmate insists, 'Treating everybody exactly the same is always the fairest thing anyone can do.' Using Fig. 5.3 and the chapter, write a reply.
questions.a: Sample: Treating people the same is a good starting point, and the right to equality does demand it in important places: everyone is equal before the law and must have equal opportunity in jobs and education. But identical treatment is not the same as a fair result. Fig. 5.3 shows three people of different heights behind a fence; giving each the same box lets the tallest see comfortably while the shortest still sees nothing. The chapter explains that providing the same thing to every individual does not provide the same benefit because of differences among people, differences that may have been carried historically from inequality and discrimination. That is why it introduces equity, the quality of being fair and just in a way that takes account of and addresses existing inequalities. So the fairest thing is sometimes to give unequal support in order to reach an equal result.
s: Concedes that equal treatment is required in the places the right to equality names
Uses Fig. 5.3 to show that identical support does not give identical benefit
Concludes with the principle of equity, addressing differences carried from past inequality

questions.q: Assertion (A): Giving the same support to every individual does not always produce the same benefit. Reason (R): People differ from one another, and those differences may be due to inequality and discrimination carried historically. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The right to equality already forbids discrimination. Analyse why the chapter still needs to introduce the separate idea of equity.
questions.a: Sample: Forbidding discrimination is a rule about what must not be done from now on: no one may be turned away because of religion, race, caste, gender or place of birth. But a rule that only stops fresh unfairness leaves untouched the gaps that earlier unfairness has already created. The chapter makes this point when it says the differences among people may be due to inequality and discrimination which may have been carried historically. If a group has been kept out of schooling for generations, simply opening the door on equal terms does not put them level with everyone else. Equity is needed because it looks at those existing inequalities and directs support at them, as the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao campaign does for girls' education. Equality removes the barrier; equity repairs the damage the barrier already did.
s: Explains that a ban on discrimination governs future conduct only
Points out that inequalities carried historically survive such a ban
Concludes that equity addresses existing inequalities, with an example such as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao

questions.q: The right to equality does three rather different things: it forbids discrimination on certain grounds, it ends untouchability, and it stops the government awarding special titles. Analyse what these three have in common.
questions.a: Sample: Each of the three attacks a way of ranking human beings. Discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, gender or place of birth ranks people by an identity they did not choose. Untouchability is the harshest form of that ranking, one carried down by custom and treating whole communities as lesser. Special titles work from the other end: instead of pushing some people below, they raise chosen individuals above the rest, and with the state's own authority behind the ranking. So the three cover ranking by birth, ranking by custom and ranking by official favour. Taken together they say that the state will neither create a hierarchy of citizens nor allow one to survive, which is what equality before the law actually requires. The single exception the chapter allows -- military or academic honours -- is telling, because those mark something a person did rather than something a person is.
s: Identifies that all three concern ranking people above or below one another
Distinguishes the ways they do so, for example by birth, by inherited custom, and by official favour
Draws the general conclusion about the state refusing a hierarchy of citizens, or explains the military and academic exception

questions.q: 'Once the law guarantees equal opportunity in jobs and education, nothing more needs to be done about inequality.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim should be rejected, though it contains something true. It is true that equal opportunity is a real guarantee of the right to equality and that without it nothing else would work. But the chapter's own argument is that providing the same thing to every individual does not provide the same benefit, because people differ and those differences may be carried historically from inequality and discrimination. A child who has never had a school in her village and a child from a family of graduates do not compete for the same seat on equal terms merely because the rule book says they may both apply. That is precisely why the chapter moves on to equity and notes the many initiatives by government and civil society organisations, such as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao. So the guarantee is necessary but not sufficient, and the claim mistakes the first step for the whole journey.
s: Accepts that equal opportunity is a genuine and necessary guarantee
Argues from the chapter that identical rules do not undo inequalities carried from the past
Reaches a clear verdict that the guarantee is necessary but not sufficient, citing equity or a named initiative

questions.q: Your school wants its annual Sports Day to be fair to every child. Propose one arrangement that follows equality and one that follows equity, explain the difference between them, and say how you would check afterwards whether the equity arrangement worked.
questions.a: Sample: An arrangement following equality would be that every child is entered for the same number of events, is given the same practice time on the field, and runs under the same rules, with no child favoured. An arrangement following equity would be that children who have no sports shoes are issued a pair from a school store, that a child who uses a wheelchair has a race designed so that he competes rather than watches, and that children who have never trained are offered extra coaching sessions in the weeks before. The difference is that the first hands out identical treatment while the second looks at what each child needs in order to actually take part, which is the chapter's definition of equity as being fair and just in a way that addresses existing inequalities. To check afterwards I would count how many children actually competed rather than how many were invited, and compare that with last year -- if the same children are still sitting out, the arrangement has not worked.
s: Proposes a workable arrangement that is genuinely equality, that is identical treatment for all
Proposes a workable arrangement that is genuinely equity, directing support by need
Explains the difference between the two in the chapter's terms
Proposes a sensible check on the outcome, such as counting who actually took part

concepts.name: The right to freedom and the right to life
concepts.description: The freedoms to express oneself, move and choose one's work, together with the reasonable restrictions that limit them; and the right to life and liberty, which the chapter extends to dignity, livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law.
concepts.idea: Freedom is not permission to do anything, and life means more than merely staying alive.
concepts.rule: The right to freedom is one of the most important rights of every Indian. It allows people to express themselves, move freely, and choose how they want to live and work. However, these freedoms are not unlimited: they come with reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or made harmful to others or to the nation. The right to life protects a person's life and liberty, and means that everyone has the right not only to live but to live with dignity. It therefore also includes the right to livelihood, education, health, a clean environment, and fair treatment under the law, so that people can live safely, freely and respectfully. The right to life also protects children with disabilities, ensuring they receive the support they need to learn, play or participate fully in all aspects of life on an equal basis with others, and that they can live with dignity and access education, healthcare and a safe environment.
concepts.example: Some countries have given rivers the same rights as people: in New Zealand the Whanganui River is legally treated as a living being, and Costa Rica protects Nature's rights in its Constitution. In 2017 the Uttarakhand High Court declared the Ganga and the Yamuna to be legal entities with the rights of a living person and appointed legal guardians to protect them, but the decision was suspended and ultimately overturned by the Supreme Court of India, which called it legally unsustainable.

questions.q: How does the chapter say the right to life protects children with disabilities?

questions.q: On Sports Day a student starts a discussion at break time about whether pupils should be allowed lighter sports clothes in hot weather. Was the student exercising freedom of speech? Give your reasons.
questions.a: Yes. The right to freedom allows people to express themselves, and raising a concern about comfort and safety in hot weather is exactly that. The student chose break time rather than disrupting a lesson, and put the point as a question for discussion rather than as a refusal to follow the rules, so the expression stayed within reasonable limits. Exercising freedom of speech does not guarantee that the opinion will be accepted, and the teachers were also entitled to remind everyone that the school's uniform rules must be followed.

questions.a: The right to a clean environment
o: The right to a clean environment
The right to education
The right to move freely

questions.q: A man is picked up by officials, held for days, and is neither told what he is accused of nor allowed to speak to anyone. Which right is at stake, and which part of it?
questions.a: The right to life is at stake, because the chapter says it protects a person's life and liberty, and liberty is exactly what has been taken here. The particular element involved is fair treatment under the law, which the chapter lists among the things the right to life includes. Because this is a fundamental right, the matter can be taken to the courts, and the right to constitutional remedies allows the Supreme Court to be approached.

questions.q: A person posts messages online that spread false rumours about a community, and fights break out in the town. He says the right to freedom protects him. Using the chapter, state whether it does, explain why, and say what principle decides the matter.
questions.a: It does not protect him. The right to freedom does allow people to express themselves, so his starting point is not absurd, but the chapter states plainly that these freedoms are not unlimited. The deciding principle is that of reasonable restrictions: a freedom may be limited so that it is not misused or made harmful to others or to the nation. Spreading falsehoods that set one community against another is precisely such harm, and the chapter adds elsewhere that actions causing harm to ourselves or others cannot be considered rights at all.
s: States clearly that the right to freedom does not protect him
Names reasonable restrictions as the deciding principle
Explains the harm to others or the nation, or cites that harmful actions cannot be rights

questions.q: A school tells a student who uses a wheelchair that she may not enter the science laboratory, saying it is for her own safety. Using the right to life, write what you would say to the school.
questions.a: Sample: The chapter says the right to life protects children with disabilities by ensuring they receive the support they need to learn, play or participate fully in all aspects of life on an equal basis with others, and that they can access education. Keeping her out of the laboratory is the opposite of that: it removes a part of her education rather than supporting it, and it does so on the ground of her disability rather than anything she has done. The right to life also means living with dignity, and being told she is a safety problem takes that away. The proper response to a genuine safety concern is to change the laboratory -- a ramp, a lowered bench, an adult assigned to assist -- exactly as ramps were built for Gaganjit at the festival, rather than to change who is allowed in.
s: Cites that the right to life requires support for children with disabilities to participate on an equal basis
Points out that exclusion removes access to education and to dignity
Proposes adapting the facility rather than excluding the student, with a supporting example

questions.q: Assertion (A): The right to freedom is not an unlimited permission to act as one pleases. Reason (R): The freedoms it grants carry reasonable restrictions so that they are not misused or made harmful to others or the nation. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The right to life is about life and liberty, yet the chapter says it includes livelihood, education, health, a clean environment and fair treatment under the law. Analyse why these are brought under it.
questions.a: Sample: They are brought under it because the chapter reads life to mean more than mere survival: everyone has the right not only to live but to live with dignity. Once dignity is the standard, each of the five follows. A person with no livelihood cannot feed herself and must depend on others to survive. Without education she cannot grow, learn and live freely. Without health or a clean environment the body is worn down by the surroundings themselves. Without fair treatment under the law she can be deprived of everything else at any moment. Each item, in other words, is a condition without which the life that remains would not be a dignified one, so protecting life seriously means protecting these as well.
s: Identifies that the chapter reads life as living with dignity, not bare survival
Shows for at least two of the items why dignity fails without them
Draws the general conclusion that these are conditions of a dignified life

questions.q: In 2017 the Uttarakhand High Court gave the Ganga and the Yamuna the rights of a living person, and the Supreme Court later overturned the order as legally unsustainable. Analyse what this episode shows about rights.
questions.a: Sample: First, it shows that the idea of who or what can hold rights is not fixed. Courts and constitutions have extended it beyond human beings, as New Zealand did for the Whanganui River and as Costa Rica does for Nature, and the Uttarakhand High Court attempted the same for the Ganga and the Yamuna, even appointing legal guardians. Second, it shows that granting a right creates a practical problem: a river cannot go to court itself, which is why guardians were needed, and working out who may speak for it is part of why the Supreme Court found the order legally unsustainable. Third, it shows that in India there is a settled way of deciding such questions. The extension was not rejected by protest or by government order but by a higher court, which is the same machinery a citizen uses under the right to constitutional remedies. The idea may well return in a better-worked form; what the episode settles is the process, not the question.
s: Notes that the holders of rights can be extended beyond human beings, with the New Zealand or Costa Rica comparison
Identifies the practical difficulty, such as who acts for the river, linked to the guardians or to the order being unsustainable
Observes that the disagreement was settled through the courts, the same route rights ordinarily take

questions.q: In the Sports Day story the teachers ended the discussion by reminding everyone that the school's uniform rules must be followed. Judge whether the student's right to freedom was respected.
questions.a: Sample: On balance it was, though the ending was unsatisfying. The student was able to raise the concern, classmates argued on both sides -- some for comfort and safety, others that the uniform shows discipline and equality among all students -- and no one was punished for speaking. That is the right to express oneself working as the chapter describes it. Being reminded that a rule stands is not the same as being silenced, and the chapter itself says freedoms carry reasonable restrictions. What is open to criticism is that the teachers closed the discussion by restating the rule rather than answering the argument; the chapter's own closing question, how should schools handle student opinions, suggests the writers think there is more to be done. A school that heard the point, explained its reasons, and reviewed the rule would respect the right more fully than one that simply ends the conversation.
s: Recognises that the student spoke freely and was not punished, so the right was exercised
Notes that a rule remaining in force is a reasonable restriction rather than a denial of the right
Offers a reasoned criticism or a better way for the school to have responded

questions.q: Write four ground rules your school could adopt for handling student opinions, so that the right to freedom is respected without school discipline collapsing. Give a brief reason for each.
questions.a: Sample: One, any student may raise a concern about a school rule, because the right to freedom allows people to express themselves and a rule no one may question is not explained, only imposed. Two, concerns are raised at a fixed time and place, such as a weekly class meeting or a suggestion box, rather than during a lesson -- the freedom is real but carries reasonable restrictions, and one student's speech should not take another's lesson. Three, the school must give a reason for its answer, not only a decision, because the Sports Day discussion showed that restating a rule settles nothing in the students' minds. Four, no student may be punished or mocked for an opinion raised in the proper way, since a freedom that is risky to use is not a freedom; a rule that is disagreed with is still followed while it stands. Together these keep the right alive and keep the school running.
s: States a rule allowing concerns to be raised, justified by the right to express oneself
States a rule about the time, place or manner, justified as a reasonable restriction
States a rule requiring the school to respond with reasons
States a rule protecting the speaker from punishment, while rules stand until changed

concepts.name: The right against exploitation and the protection of children
concepts.description: What exploitation means and the forms it takes, why children need special protection, the limits the chapter states on employing children below fourteen, and the Childline 1098 helpline with the 2015 rescue it describes.
concepts.idea: Exploitation is taking unfair advantage of someone who is in no position to refuse, and children are the least able to refuse of all.
concepts.rule: Exploitation means taking unfair advantage of others, often by denying them basic respect, liberty and rights. It can happen in many ways: when people are forced to work without fair wages, which is bonded labour; when they are traded or sold for profit, which is human trafficking; when women or children are abused or treated unfairly; and when children are made to work instead of going to school, particularly in hazardous situations, which is child labour. Children need special protection because they depend on adults for their safety and wellbeing, and may not understand their rights, or be able to stand up for themselves, or access help against unfair treatment or unsafe situations. When children are made to work they lose out on education, play and a healthy childhood, things that are essential for their growth and future. The right against exploitation protects every person's dignity and safety and makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will or under unsafe conditions. In general children below the age of 14 are not allowed to be employed, though they can help out in non-hazardous family enterprises, and only during vacations or after school hours; there is a ban on work in places such as factories, mines or restaurants.
concepts.example: The government runs a helpline for children, Childline 1098, available all over the country and easy to remember by counting backwards from 10. In 2015 it received a call from a concerned citizen about 20 children being forced to work in a factory that embroidered clothes. A team visited, found the children in a congested and unhealthy room and fed only once a day on food that was not nourishing, rescued them, provided medical care and ensured they would be looked after; the culprits were arrested.

questions.q: You notice a child of about ten clearing tables at a roadside eating place on a school morning. Using the chapter, state two things you could do.
questions.a: First, I could speak to my teacher or my principal, which the chapter suggests as a step a student can take, so that an adult with some authority knows and can act. Second, I could contact the children's helpline, Childline 1098, which is available all over the country; the chapter describes a concerned citizen doing exactly this in 2015, after which a team visited the place and the children were rescued.

questions.q: A girl of thirteen helps at her family's vegetable stall for two hours on Sunday mornings during the school holidays. Does the chapter treat this as child labour? Explain.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that although children below 14 are generally not allowed to be employed, they can help out in non-hazardous family enterprises, and only during vacations or after school hours. A family vegetable stall is a family enterprise and is not hazardous, and the help is given during the holidays, so all three conditions are met. What would change the answer is if the work were hazardous, if it were for an outside employer, or if it kept her away from school.
s: Answers that this is not child labour under the chapter's rule

questions.q: Describe the 2015 Childline case: what the call was about, what the team found, and what was done afterwards.
questions.a: A concerned citizen telephoned Childline 1098 to report that 20 children were being forced to work in a factory that embroidered clothes. A team visited the place and found the children there; not only were they being forced to work, but the room they worked in was congested and unhealthy, and the food they were given once a day was not nourishing at all. The team rescued the children, provided them with medical care and made sure they would be taken care of afterwards, and the culprits were arrested.
s: States that a concerned citizen called about 20 children forced to work in an embroidery factory
Describes the conditions found: congested and unhealthy room, one unnourishing meal a day
States that the children were rescued and given medical care, and the culprits arrested

questions.q: A shopkeeper says that employing a twelve-year-old from a poor family is really a kindness, because the family badly needs the money. Using the chapter, write your reply.
questions.a: Sample: The need is real, but what he is offering is not the remedy he thinks it is. The chapter says children below 14 are generally not to be employed, and that when children are made to work they lose out on education, play and a healthy childhood, all essential to their growth and future. So the wage helps the family this month while costing the child the schooling that is her only way out of poverty later; the kindness is short and the damage is long. The chapter also warns that children may not understand their rights or be able to stand up for themselves, which is exactly why an arrangement they cannot refuse counts as exploitation even when the employer means no harm. If he genuinely wants to help, he could support the family in a way that keeps the child in school -- which is what the volunteers at the festival did when they had the working children enrolled.
s: Acknowledges the family's real need rather than dismissing it
Argues that working costs the child education, play and a healthy childhood, harming her future
Notes that children cannot properly refuse, or proposes help that keeps the child in school

questions.q: Assertion (A): Children need a special protection against exploitation that adults do not need in the same way. Reason (R): Children depend on adults for their safety and wellbeing, and may not understand their rights or be able to stand up for themselves. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: A child under 14 may help in a family enterprise but may not work in a factory, a mine or a restaurant. Analyse the reasoning behind drawing the line in that place.
questions.a: Sample: The line is drawn by asking who holds the power and what the work costs the child. In a family enterprise the child is among people responsible for her wellbeing, so she is unlikely to be worked to exhaustion or refused food, and the chapter still fences the permission with two conditions: the work must be non-hazardous and must fall in vacations or after school hours, so that schooling is untouched. A factory, a mine or a restaurant fails on both counts. The child is under an employer whose interest is the work rather than the child, which is precisely the imbalance the chapter calls taking unfair advantage; and such work runs through the day, so it replaces school rather than fitting around it. The conditions in the 2015 embroidery factory -- a congested, unhealthy room and one poor meal a day -- show what the outer line is protecting against.
s: Explains that in a family enterprise the adults are responsible for the child's wellbeing
Notes the conditions attached: non-hazardous and outside school hours, so education is preserved
Explains why an outside employer differs, citing the imbalance of power or the 2015 factory conditions

questions.q: In the 2015 embroidery factory case, several different things had to happen before the children were actually safe. Identify them and explain why no single one of them would have been enough on its own.
questions.a: Sample: First a citizen had to notice and telephone: without the call nothing would have begun, since the children themselves could not seek help, which is the chapter's reason for saying children need special protection. Second the helpline had to exist and be reachable across the country, so that the call led somewhere. Third a team had to actually visit and find the children, turning a report into evidence. Fourth the children had to be removed and given medical care, because after a congested, unhealthy room and one poor meal a day, simply setting them free would have left them hurt and unfed. Fifth someone had to ensure they would be taken care of afterwards, or they would have drifted back to the same work. Sixth the culprits had to be arrested, or the factory would have filled with other children within a week. Each step fails without the others: a call without a visit is a complaint, a rescue without aftercare is abandonment, and a rescue without arrests changes nothing for the next child.
s: Identifies at least four distinct steps, from the citizen's call through to the arrests
Explains why the early steps alone are insufficient, for example a call without a visit or evidence
Explains why rescue alone is insufficient, citing aftercare or the arrest of the culprits

questions.q: 'A telephone helpline is a weak way to protect children, because a helpline cannot rescue anybody.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim misunderstands what the helpline is for, though it starts from a fair observation. It is true that the number itself rescues no one; in the 2015 case it was a team that visited, found the children and removed them. But the difficulty the chapter identifies is that children may not understand their rights, may be unable to stand up for themselves, and may not be able to access help at all. A helpline solves exactly that: it is free, national, and so easy to remember that a child, or a passer-by like the concerned citizen in 2015, can start the process without knowing which office to approach. Without that first call the team would never have gone. So the helpline is not a substitute for rescue but the door to it, and judging it by whether it performs the rescue itself is judging it by the wrong test.
s: Concedes the true part, that the helpline itself does not carry out the rescue
Argues that its value is in making help accessible to children or bystanders who would not know where to turn
Reaches a clear verdict, supported by the 2015 case where the call set everything in motion

questions.q: Design a small poster for your classroom wall headed 'If you see a child working'. Include the helpline number with its memory trick, two steps a student can take, and one line explaining why this is a matter of rights and not only of kindness.
questions.a: Sample: Heading -- If you see a child working. The number: Childline 1098, free and available all over India; to remember it, just count backwards from 10. Step one: tell a teacher or the principal the same day, with the place and the time you saw the child, because an adult can act on what you noticed. Step two: make the call to 1098, or ask an adult to make it with you -- in 2015 one concerned citizen's call led to 20 children being rescued from an embroidery factory and the culprits being arrested. Why this is about rights: the right against exploitation makes it illegal to force anyone to work against their will or in unsafe conditions, and a child made to work loses education, play and a healthy childhood. Reporting it is not charity towards that child; it is the protection the Constitution already promises her.
s: Gives the number 1098 with the counting-backwards memory trick
Gives a first workable step, such as telling a teacher or principal
Gives a second workable step, such as calling the helpline, ideally supported by the 2015 case
Explains that this engages the right against exploitation, not merely kindness

concepts.name: Freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights
concepts.description: The freedom to choose, practise and share a religion together with the bar on forcing anyone to follow, propagate or fund one; the rule that state-run and government-aided schools may not promote a particular religion; and the rights protecting language, script, traditions and minority institutions.
concepts.idea: The state keeps all faiths equal in its own eyes, and at the same time lets communities keep what makes them different.
concepts.rule: India is a diverse country where people follow many different religions. The right to freedom of religion allows every person to choose, practise and share their religion freely, while ensuring that no one is forced to follow, propagate or fund a particular religion. At the same time, state-run or government-aided schools are not allowed to promote any particular religion; this helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. Cultural and educational rights protect India's rich cultural diversity and ensure equal access to education for all. Communities can preserve their language, script and traditions, and no student can be denied admission to a government institution because of religion, caste, race or language. Religious and linguistic minorities also have the right to set up and manage their own schools. These rights help maintain cultural identity while supporting equality and non-discrimination. Fig. 5.2 places freedom of religion in Articles 25-28 and cultural and educational rights in Articles 29 and 30.
concepts.example: The chapter notes that these two aims can at times seem to be in conflict: on one hand the Constitution seeks to protect the rights of minorities, and on the other it upholds equality and non-discrimination on the basis of religion, so some people feel that minority protections -- the special rights and safeguards given to groups with a different religion, language or culture -- may go against the idea of secularism.

questions.q: A small community finds its traditional script is dying out and wants to run classes and publish books in it. State whether the chapter gives them a right to do so, name the right and its article range from Fig. 5.2, and state one thing this right does not give them.

It falls under cultural and educational rights, which Fig. 5.2 places in Articles 29 and 30, and which say that communities can preserve their language, script and traditions. What the right does not give them is any power over other people: they may not require anyone else to learn the script, and if they set up a school of their own they still cannot deny admission to a student on the ground of religion, caste, race or language, since the same rights uphold equality and non-discrimination.

questions.q: A friend asks, 'If the state already treats every religion equally, why should minorities be allowed their own schools at all?' Using the chapter, write your answer.
questions.a: Sample: Equal treatment by the state and protection for minorities are answers to two different dangers. The first danger is that the state might favour one faith, and the chapter blocks it by barring state-run and government-aided schools from promoting any particular religion, so that all faiths are equal in its eyes. The second danger is that a small community's language, script and traditions simply disappear, not because anyone attacked them but because every institution around them belongs to the majority. Equal treatment does nothing about that, so the Constitution adds cultural and educational rights, letting communities preserve their language, script and traditions and letting religious and linguistic minorities set up and manage their own schools. The chapter is honest that the two aims can seem to conflict and that some people see minority protections as against secularism. But the school does not take anything from anyone else; it only stops the smaller community from being absorbed, which is what protecting India's rich cultural diversity means.
s: Explains that the bar on state schools promoting a religion is what keeps faiths equal in the state's eyes
Explains the separate danger that a minority's language, script and traditions may disappear
Acknowledges the tension the chapter admits, and still gives a reasoned answer

questions.q: Assertion (A): State-run and government-aided schools in India may not promote any particular religion. Reason (R): This helps protect India's diversity and keeps all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Why do you think the Constitution treats cultural rights and educational rights as one category rather than two separate ones? Analyse using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: Because a culture is passed on mainly through teaching, so the two cannot be separated in practice. A community's language, script and traditions survive only if children learn them, and children learn them in schools; that is why the same category both protects the language and script and gives minorities the right to set up and manage their own schools. The pairing also works the other way. Education is the very place where a culture is most easily denied, which is why the same rights say no student may be refused admission to a government institution on grounds of religion, caste, race or language. So one category covers both the thing to be protected and the main means by which it is protected or destroyed, and that is why the chapter can say these rights safeguard cultural identity while promoting equal access to education in a single sentence.
s: Explains that culture is transmitted through education, so schools are how language and traditions survive
Notes that education is also where a culture or a community can be excluded, hence the admission rule
Concludes that the category covers both what is protected and the means of protecting it

questions.q: The chapter admits that protecting minority rights and upholding non-discrimination on the basis of religion can seem to pull against each other. Analyse this tension and suggest how it might be resolved.
questions.a: Sample: The tension is real. Non-discrimination says the state should not sort people by religion at all; minority protections require the state to notice who is a minority in order to give them safeguards, which is why some people argue these protections go against the idea of secularism. The apparent contradiction dissolves once we ask what each rule is for. Non-discrimination exists to stop people being held back because of their religion, language or culture. Minority protections exist for the same purpose, in a situation where treating everyone identically would not produce an equal result -- which is the chapter's own distinction between equality and equity applied to culture rather than to boxes at a fence. A safeguard that lets a small community keep its school is not a privilege over others; it is what stops the community being absorbed. The resolution, then, is to judge such protections by whether they secure equal standing or hand out an advantage, and to withdraw them when the second is true. The chapter does not settle the argument, and says only that the two aims can seem to conflict.
s: States the tension accurately: non-discrimination ignores religion while minority protection must notice it
Argues that both aims share the purpose of preventing people being held back, linking to equity if possible
Offers a reasoned resolution or test, while noting the chapter leaves the argument open

questions.q: 'The right to freedom of religion is enough by itself; cultural and educational rights add nothing that it does not already cover.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim should be rejected. The two rights do overlap, which is why it is tempting: both protect a community's way of life, and a minority school often serves a religious community. But freedom of religion is about belief and worship -- choosing, practising and sharing a religion, and not being forced to follow, propagate or fund one. Cultural and educational rights reach things that have nothing to do with belief. A language and a script are not religious; a linguistic minority that shares the majority's religion is protected by the second right and not by the first. The rule that no student may be denied admission to a government institution on grounds of caste, race or language is likewise outside religion altogether. So the claim leaves unprotected exactly the cases the chapter cares about when it speaks of India's rich cultural diversity, which is wider than its religious diversity.
s: Identifies what freedom of religion covers: belief, worship, and freedom from compulsion
Shows something cultural and educational rights cover that religion does not, such as language, script or linguistic minorities
Reaches a clear verdict rejecting the claim, while acknowledging the genuine overlap

questions.q: You are asked to draw up the festival policy for a government school. Write four rules that respect both the freedom of religion and the bar on a state school promoting any particular religion, giving a reason for each.
questions.a: Sample: One, no festival of any single faith may be made a compulsory school event, because a state-run school is not allowed to promote a particular religion. Two, the school may hold one Festivals of India day at which students present the festivals of every community in the school, since the aim is to protect India's diversity and keep all faiths equal in the eyes of the state. Three, no student may be asked to contribute money towards any religious celebration, as the chapter states that no one may be forced to fund a particular religion. Four, any student who prefers not to take part in a presentation may step aside without being questioned or mocked, because the right includes the freedom not to follow or propagate a religion, and pressure from classmates would be discrimination on religious grounds. These four together let the school notice religion without preferring one.
s: Gives a rule preventing the school from making one faith's festival an official event
Gives a rule allowing all communities' festivals to be recognised equally
Gives a rule on not requiring funding for a religion

concepts.name: Fundamental duties, and rights and duties as two sides of the same coin
concepts.description: What fundamental duties are, when and how they entered the Constitution, the eleven duties of Article 51A with the chapter's everyday examples, the ancient ideas of dharma, rina and adhikara, and how duties differ from rights while going together with them.
concepts.idea: Rights and duties are not opposites: every right a citizen enjoys has a matching duty that keeps it real for everybody else.
concepts.rule: The Constitution not only gives rights, it also tells citizens what they should do; these responsibilities are called fundamental duties, and the idea behind including them was to remind citizens of their duties alongside enjoying their fundamental rights. When the Constitution came into effect in 1950 it had no Fundamental Duties. They were added in 1976 by an amendment, at first as 10 duties listed in Article 51A, which is Part IV-A; in 2002 an 11th was added, requiring parents or guardians to make sure children between 6 and 14 years get an education. The eleven are: abide by and respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem; follow the ideals of the freedom struggle; protect India's unity, integrity and sovereignty; defend the nation and help in emergencies; promote harmony among all people and respect women; preserve culture and heritage; protect and improve the environment and have compassion towards animals; develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry; protect public property and avoid violence; strive for excellence in all activities; and ensure education for children aged 6 to 14. Rights are the freedoms and benefits every citizen enjoys and duties are the responsibilities we follow as members of a community; they are not opposites but go together. Rights are protected by law, so a person whose rights are violated, even by the government, can go to court for help, whereas duties are moral and social responsibilities that we are expected to follow, though not doing so may not always lead to legal action.
concepts.example: Every right has a matching duty: if I have the right to be treated with respect, I also have the duty to treat others with respect; and if I have the right to express my opinions freely, I have the duty to listen to and respect other people's views, even when I disagree, and to do so without causing harm.

questions.q: Explain what the chapter means by saying that every right has a matching duty, using one of its own examples.
questions.a: It means that a right held by one person only works if everyone else accepts a corresponding responsibility, so the two always come in pairs. The chapter's own example is speech: if I have the right to express my opinions freely, I have the duty to listen to and respect other people's views, even when I disagree, and to do so without causing harm. If I claimed the right but refused the duty, I would be demanding a freedom for myself that I deny to everybody else.
s: Explains that a right for one person implies a matching responsibility on others, so the two go in pairs
Gives one of the chapter's pairs correctly, such as respect, or free expression with the duty to listen

o: Protect and improve the environment and have compassion towards animals

Preserve culture and heritage

questions.q: After losing a football match some boys want to break the school benches, and their classmates stop them. Name the Fundamental Duty involved and explain how the classmates upheld it.
questions.a: The duty involved is to protect public property and avoid violence. The classmates upheld it by reminding the angry boys that the benches were school property, belonging to everyone rather than to the losing team, and by pointing out that winning and losing are both part of sports, so the disappointment gave them no licence to damage what others depend on.

Explains how the classmates acted, for example reminding them the benches were school property

questions.q: In a flood-hit village, NCC cadets rescue stranded people and distribute food packets. The chapter gives this as an example of which duty?

o: Defend the nation and help in emergencies
