questions.q: A group of students, not satisfied with memorising their notes on the purification of water, go and show a disadvantaged community how to filter water and then boil it. Name the duty involved and say what the example adds to it.
questions.a: The duty is to develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry. The example adds that scientific temper is not shown by learning the topic well but by asking what the knowledge is actually for: the students were not content with memorising, so they turned a lesson into something that made other people's drinking water safe. It shows the duty being performed through use and curiosity rather than through examination marks.
s: Names the duty to develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry
Explains that the example shows knowledge being put to use rather than merely memorised

questions.q: Ravi decides not to join a protest march at school because he disagrees with it, and some classmates say they will exclude him from their group unless he joins. Name the right Ravi is exercising, the duty his classmates are failing, and say what ought to happen.
questions.a: Ravi is exercising the right to freedom, which allows people to express themselves and to choose how they want to live; choosing not to speak is as much a part of free expression as choosing to speak. His classmates are failing the matching duty the chapter states, to listen to and respect other people's views even when they disagree, and their threat to exclude him is a form of discrimination. What ought to happen is that the group accepts his decision without penalty and argues with his reasons if they wish, since agreeing with a march cannot be the price of belonging to a friendship group.
s: Names the right to freedom, or the freedom to express oneself, including the freedom not to join
Names the duty to listen to and respect others' views even when disagreeing
States what ought to happen, that Ravi is accepted without penalty for his choice

questions.q: A student argues, 'I have the right to express my opinions freely, so I may say whatever I like about anybody.' Using the chapter's idea of matching duties, write a reply.
questions.a: Sample: The right is real, but the sentence leaves out the half that goes with it. The chapter says that if I have the right to express my opinions freely, I have the duty to listen to and respect other people's views, even when I disagree, and to do so without causing harm. Those last three words settle the argument: a remark aimed at humiliating somebody is not an opinion being expressed but harm being done, and the chapter states elsewhere that actions causing harm to others cannot be rights at all, and that freedoms carry reasonable restrictions. There is also a plain consistency problem. He is claiming a freedom for himself that he is not willing to extend to the person he insults, and a right claimed on those terms is not a right but a privilege. Gandhi's line at the head of the chapter puts it shortest: the true source of rights is duty.
s: States the matching duty: to listen to and respect others' views without causing harm
Argues that harmful speech falls outside the right, citing harm or reasonable restrictions
Points out the inconsistency of claiming a freedom one will not extend to others, or cites Gandhi's line

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fundamental Duties are not enforced in the way Fundamental Rights are. Reason (R): Duties are moral and social responsibilities, and not performing them may not always lead to legal action. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter describes the ancient Indian idea of rina, or debt. Analyse what it meant and how it differs from today's sense of duty.
questions.a: Sample: Rina means debt, and the idea is that by the very fact of being born a person already owes something: debts to devatas, to ancestors and parents, to gurus, to fellow humans and to Nature. The duty of repaying those debts then follows naturally, so duty is not imposed from outside but arises from what one has already received. The chapter says this is more than today's sense of duty, and the difference is worth drawing out. A modern duty is usually a rule addressed to a citizen, something to be complied with, and it can in principle be listed and ticked off. Rina is a relationship rather than a rule: it creates deep connections with family, society, Nature and beyond, and a debt of that kind is never finished, only honoured. The chapter also notes that dharma, often translated as duty, has a much wider range of meaning, including what is beneficial to people and to society, which points the same way.
s: Explains rina as debt owed from birth, naming several of the creditors listed
States that repaying the debts is what makes duty follow naturally
Draws a real contrast with the modern sense of duty, such as relationship versus rule, or never finished versus complied with

questions.q: The chapter says that in ancient texts adhikara meant capacity, competence or authority, while today it is the word for rights. Analyse what changed, and why the change matters.
questions.a: Sample: In the older usage a person's adhikara followed from what they were competent to do: being able to perform a certain task in society was what gave them the right to do it. Rights were therefore earned, particular and unequal, because they depended on one's capacity, and a person judged to lack the capacity simply had no claim. What changed is the ground on which a right rests. Under the Constitution rights are guaranteed universally, held because a person is a human being and a member of society, not because anyone has assessed what they can do. The change matters because the older arrangement gave nothing to exactly the people who needed protection most -- the child, the person with a disability, anyone a society had decided was not competent -- and it could be used to justify keeping them out. The chapter records one exception, that dharma implicitly gave everyone the right to justice, and is careful to add the words in theory at least, which suggests the exception did not always hold in practice.
s: Explains the older meaning: adhikara as capacity or competence, so rights depended on what one could do
Contrasts it with rights today being guaranteed universally regardless of capacity
Explains why this matters, for example that the old basis excluded those least able to claim, and notes the dharma exception

questions.q: The chapter asks: can we demand rights without doing our duties? Give your judgement, using the chapter and the line at the head of it.
questions.a: Sample: In the narrow legal sense we can. Rights are protected by law and can be enforced in court, while duties are moral and social responsibilities whose breach may not always lead to legal action, so a citizen who neglects every duty does not thereby lose his rights -- and that is deliberate, because rights that could be withdrawn for bad behaviour would protect nobody when they were most needed. But in the sense the chapter cares about, the answer is no. Fulfilling our duties is what protects everyone's rights and keeps society fair and peaceful, so a society where everyone demanded and nobody contributed would leave the rights formally intact and practically worthless: my right to be treated with respect exists only because others accept the duty to respect me. That is what the chapter means by two sides of the same coin, and what Gandhi means at the head of the chapter when he says the true source of rights is duty. So we may demand them, but we could not long enjoy them.
s: Distinguishes the legal position, that rights are enforceable and are not forfeited by neglecting duties
Argues that in practice rights depend on others performing matching duties
Reaches a clear judgement, supported by the two-sides idea or by Gandhi's line

questions.q: Write four right-and-duty pairs for a classroom charter. Each pair should state a right a student has and the matching duty it places on everyone else, and one of the four should deal with disagreement.
questions.a: Sample: One -- every student has the right to be heard in class discussion; the matching duty is that the rest of us stay quiet and let her finish, since a right to speak is worth nothing in a room where nobody listens. Two -- every student has the right to disagree with an opinion, including the teacher's, without being excluded for it; the matching duty is to listen to and respect other people's views even when we disagree, and to argue with the opinion rather than the person, as Ravi's classmates failed to do when they threatened to drop him. Three -- every student has the right to a clean and safe classroom; the matching duty is that each of us puts our own wrappers in the dustbin rather than on the floor, which is the duty to protect and improve the environment. Four -- every student has the right to use the class books, sports gear and furniture; the matching duty is to protect public property, so no one damages what belongs to all of us. Each pair follows the chapter's rule that a right for one person is a responsibility for everybody else.
s: Gives a first workable pair in which the duty genuinely matches the right
Gives a second workable pair with a genuine matching duty
Includes a pair dealing with disagreement, resting on the duty to listen to and respect other views
Gives a fourth pair and shows understanding that a right for one is a responsibility for others

concepts.name: Discrimination, visible and invisible
concepts.description: What discrimination is and on what grounds it happens, the harm it does to the person and to society, the examples of Savitribai Phule and Anandibai Joshi, and the indirect forms that are hard to prove and therefore hard to penalise.
concepts.idea: Most discrimination is not a rule that shuts a door; it is a whisper, a nickname or an invitation that never comes.
concepts.rule: Discrimination is mistreating any person or group because of their caste, religion, ethnicity, disability, race, physical appearance, gender, sexuality or economic background. It is not only unethical but also legally prohibited. Discriminating against someone on these grounds impacts the affected person or group both psychologically and physically, and also impacts society as a whole. It can be as subtle as not talking to a classmate or not including them in a group project because of their social or economic background, or not letting someone sit next to you in a school bus. Discrimination creates a social barrier on those subjected to it, hampering them from enjoying their fundamental rights; and someone who discriminates ethically ceases to be an active citizen of India, because they have breached the very core of the Indian Constitution, that is respect and unity. Discrimination may not always be visible: it may be indirect, through taking a jibe at somebody, excluding someone, or being unwilling to include someone in a project or a celebration just because of their social background, physical appearance or perception of intellectual ability. The major issue with invisible discrimination is that it is difficult to prove, and hence difficult to penalise.
concepts.example: In the mid-19th century Savitribai Phule established a school for girls at a time when people believed girls should not go to school. What appalled them even more was that she was from a so-called lower caste, the Mali community. She was abused and mud was thrown at her on her way to school, yet she remained steadfast, and together with her husband Jyotiba Phule she worked to ensure that girls and children from all backgrounds had access to education.

questions.q: Mina did not enrol for the overnight school trip because her family could not afford it, and some friends then began ignoring her and whispering that she 'was not of their status'. Identify the ground of discrimination and say whether this is visible or invisible discrimination.
questions.a: The ground is her economic background, since it was her family's inability to pay for the trip that set the whole thing off. It is invisible, or indirect, discrimination: nobody announced a rule or openly barred her from anything, and the mistreatment took the form of being ignored and whispered about, which is exactly the sort of exclusion the chapter says is hard to prove.
s: Identifies economic background as the ground
Classifies it as invisible or indirect discrimination, working through exclusion and whispering rather than an open rule

questions.q: Some students laugh at Rukmini for wearing her family's traditional dress on School Culture Day and tell her she should wear 'modern' clothes. According to the chapter's closing summary, discrimination based on personal preferences such as choice of clothing is
questions.a: Against fundamental rights
o: Against fundamental rights

Outside the chapter's definition of discrimination

questions.q: A boy in your class is never picked for group projects because of his economic background, though nobody ever says so aloud. Explain why this is hard to act against.
questions.a: Because it is invisible discrimination. There is no rule to point to and no statement anybody made; each group simply formed without him, and every single choice can be explained away as coincidence or friendship. The chapter says the major issue with invisible discrimination is that it is difficult to prove and hence difficult to penalise, even though the harm to the boy -- being shut out again and again -- is just as real as an open refusal.
s: Identifies it as invisible or indirect discrimination, with no rule or statement to point to
Explains that it is therefore difficult to prove and to penalise, though the harm is real

questions.q: Compare the case of Rohan with the case of Mina. Say which is the more visible, which the more invisible, and explain why the difference matters.
questions.a: Rohan's case is the more visible: the group calls him 'Drummy' out loud, jokes that he would be competing with the football, and the chapter notes that everyone around notices this behaviour. Mina's case is the more invisible: nobody bars her from anything, and the mistreatment is being ignored and whispered about after she quietly does not enrol for the trip. The difference matters because a teacher can act on Rohan's case at once, having seen and heard it, whereas Mina's exclusion leaves nothing to point to; each friend can say she simply drifted away. That is why the chapter says invisible discrimination is difficult to prove and hence difficult to penalise, and why it has to be noticed deliberately rather than waited for.
s: Identifies Rohan's case as visible, with the open nickname and jokes noticed by everyone
Identifies Mina's case as invisible, working through being ignored and whispered about
Explains why the difference matters, that the invisible kind is hard to prove and to act upon

questions.q: Sanya was told by some students that she did not 'fit the image' of a lead actor. Nobody actually prevented her from auditioning, and she won an important role anyway. Explain why the drama teacher still called this discrimination.
questions.a: Sample: Because discrimination is mistreating a person because of something like their physical appearance, and that is exactly what the whispering did: it judged her by her looks rather than by her acting, and pushed her towards a smaller role on that basis. It does not stop being discrimination because it failed. The chapter records that Sanya felt discouraged, which is the psychological harm it names, and a less determined student would simply have withdrawn -- in which case nobody would ever have known what was lost, and the unfairness would have been invisible. This is the indirect kind the chapter describes, working through a jibe and through discouragement rather than a rule. The teacher was right to name it, because the students needed to learn that talent and effort matter far more than appearance before the next audition, not after somebody had been driven off.
s: Identifies physical appearance as the ground, and judging by looks rather than ability as the wrong
Explains that the harm is real even though she succeeded, citing that she felt discouraged
Notes that a less determined student would have withdrawn, or that this is the indirect kind that must be named

questions.q: Assertion (A): Invisible discrimination is difficult to penalise. Reason (R): It works through jibes, exclusion and an unwillingness to include people, none of which is easy to prove. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The chapter says discrimination affects not only the person discriminated against but society as a whole. Analyse why this is so.
questions.a: Sample: The first loss is to the person, psychologically and physically, and the chapter adds that discrimination creates a social barrier that hampers them from enjoying their fundamental rights -- so the harm is not only hurt feelings but rights made unusable in practice. The loss to society follows in several ways. What is wasted is talent: had Sanya been discouraged from auditioning, the play would simply have had a worse lead, and a country that keeps girls or a caste out of schooling never finds out what they might have contributed. There is also a loss of trust, since people who expect to be shut out stop putting themselves forward, and the exclusion then looks self-confirming. Finally the chapter's own point is that the discriminator breaches the core of the Constitution, respect and unity, so each act chips at the shared understanding that holds a diverse country together. Discrimination is therefore not a private quarrel between two people; it removes something the whole society was relying on.
s: States the harm to the individual, psychological and physical, and the barrier to enjoying fundamental rights
Explains a loss to society, such as wasted talent or withdrawal of those who expect exclusion
Links it to the breach of respect and unity at the core of the Constitution

questions.q: Analyse the story of Anandibai Joshi as an account of discrimination: what she faced, what it cost her, and what the chapter wants a reader to take from it.
questions.a: Sample: What she faced began before she could have chosen anything: she was married in 1874 at the age of nine, and by fifteen she was a mother whose baby died soon after birth for want of medical care. That loss set her course -- she decided to study medicine so that she could serve mothers and children -- and it also shows that the harm here was not only insult but a shortage of care for women that cost a life. When she resolved to go to the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania, people were aghast; the chapter says she fought discrimination and sustained considerable hardship to realise her dream. What it cost her was almost everything, since she succumbed to an illness soon after graduating and her dream was left unfulfilled. The chapter places her beside Savitribai Phule for a reason. Both faced the belief that women had no business seeking education, both were determined, and neither had an easy victory. The lesson is not a comfortable one about effort always being rewarded; it is that discrimination exacts a real price, and that the people who pushed against it did so knowing this.
s: Sets out what she faced: child marriage at nine, motherhood at fifteen, the baby's death for lack of medical care, and people aghast at her going abroad
States the cost: considerable hardship, and death from illness soon after graduating with her dream unfulfilled
Draws a reasoned lesson, for example the comparison with Savitribai Phule or the real price of resisting discrimination

questions.q: 'Since invisible discrimination cannot be proved, there is nothing that can usefully be done about it.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Sample: The claim takes a true premise and draws a false conclusion. It is true, and the chapter says so, that the major issue with invisible discrimination is that it is difficult to prove and hence difficult to penalise; a school cannot punish a class for friendships that never formed. But penalty is not the only remedy available. The chapter's own examples are settled without anyone being punished at all: the drama teacher simply names what happened to Sanya and talks to the class about it, and the students conclude that talent and effort matter more than appearance. The caselets on Rohan and Mina are set as discussion tasks for exactly that reason -- they ask what you would do if you were part of the group. Inclusion works the same way, by removing barriers rather than proving offences, as when Smt. Amita widened the reading club instead of finding someone to blame. So the honest conclusion is that invisible discrimination is hard to punish and must therefore be met by noticing, naming and changing behaviour, which is harder than a penalty but not nothing.
s: Accepts the true premise that invisible discrimination is hard to prove and to penalise
Rejects the conclusion by showing remedies other than punishment, such as naming it or discussion
Supports the argument with a chapter example, such as the drama teacher, the caselets, or the reading club

questions.q: Write four questions a class could ask itself once a term to check whether invisible discrimination is happening in the classroom. For each, say what an honest answer would reveal.
questions.a: Sample: One -- when we form project groups, is there anyone who is always chosen last, or left for the teacher to place? An honest answer reveals exclusion by social or economic background, the kind that hides behind ordinary friendship. Two -- does anyone in this class have a nickname they did not choose, and what is it about? An honest answer reveals jibes about physical appearance, as Rohan's 'Drummy' did. Three -- when an activity costs money, do we find out quietly who cannot pay, or do we let them make an excuse? An honest answer reveals whether we are repeating what happened to Mina, who was left to say nothing and then judged for it. Four -- who has not spoken in class this week, and do we know why? An honest answer reveals students being talked over because of a perception of their intellectual ability, or because they take longer to read or write. These are all questions about patterns rather than incidents, because invisible discrimination shows up in patterns and never in a single provable act.
s: Gives a first question that would surface exclusion from groups or activities
Gives a second question targeting jibes or nicknames about appearance
Gives a third question addressing economic background without exposing the student
Gives a fourth question and shows awareness that the check is for patterns, not single provable acts

concepts.name: Inclusion, and removing barriers to participation
concepts.description: Inclusion as an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected and valued with equal access to opportunities; why it goes beyond reservations; the reading club that grew once it widened; and the difference between handing out support and removing the barrier itself.
concepts.idea: Equity shares out help so people can get over the barrier; inclusion asks why the barrier is there at all.
concepts.rule: Inclusion means creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities. This is especially important for groups that have historically been excluded because of their social or economic background. Inclusion goes beyond just giving reservations; it means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported, and in the Constitution fundamental rights and duties together support inclusion. In practice it can mean finding ways for people speaking different languages to communicate, welcoming students from all castes, religions or backgrounds into schools, and giving extra help such as braille books, ramps or classroom support to children with special needs. It also means removing barriers to participation. The chapter defines inclusion as ensuring no one is left out because of language, religion, culture, ethnicity, caste or gender, and calls it an affirmative way to ensure non-discrimination. The chapter's closing points add that deliberate actions need to be taken to prevent discrimination and ensure inclusion, and that democracy is strengthened through enabling and facilitating the participation of all.

questions.q: For which groups does the chapter say inclusion is especially important, and why?
questions.a: It says inclusion is especially important for groups that have historically been excluded because of their social or economic background. The reason is that their exclusion was not a single recent act but something carried over a long time, so simply stopping the mistreatment now leaves them still outside; they need to be actively welcomed, supported and given equal access to opportunities before they can take part on the same footing as everyone else.

questions.q: The chapter asks you to compare Fig. 5.14 with Fig. 5.3. What difference is there between them?

In Fig. 5.14 there are no boxes at all, because the barrier itself has been taken away and all three watch the match directly. The difference is that equality and equity work around an obstacle, while inclusion removes the obstacle, which is what the chapter means by removing barriers to participation.

questions.q: Retell the story of Smt. Amita's reading club: the problem she faced, the change she made, the result, and the principle it demonstrates.
questions.a: The problem was that fewer books were being borrowed from the library, so she started a reading club to get students back into the habit of reading, but only a few confident readers of English joined it. The change she made was to expand the scope of the club to include books in the regional language. The result was that membership soon increased, the club's activities grew to include storytelling and puppetry from the region, and all children began to participate irrespective of their fluency in a particular language. The principle it demonstrates is inclusion: rather than blaming the students who stayed away, she removed the barrier that was keeping them out, which is what creating an environment where everyone has equal access to opportunities means.

questions.q: A school principal says, 'Our doors are open to every child without exception, so our school is already fully inclusive.' Using the chapter, write your response.
questions.a: Sample: An open door is where inclusion starts, not where it finishes. The chapter defines inclusion as creating an environment where everyone feels welcomed, respected, valued and included, with equal access to opportunities, and says plainly that it goes beyond just giving reservations and means making sure everyone feels accepted and supported. Smt. Amita's reading club was open to every student too, and only a few confident readers of English came; the door was not the barrier, the language was. In the same way a school with no ramp is open to a child who uses a wheelchair only in the sense that nobody has forbidden her to come, which is exactly Gaganjit's position at the festival exhibition hall. The real test is not who is permitted to enter but who is actually taking part, so I would ask the principal to look at who is missing from the clubs, the trips and the discussions, and then to remove whatever is keeping them out.
s: Argues that an open door is only the beginning, citing the chapter's fuller definition of inclusion
Supports this with an example such as the reading club, the ramp, or Gaganjit
Proposes the real test: who actually participates, and removing the barriers that keep others out

questions.q: Using Fig. 5.3 and Fig. 5.14, analyse the difference between equality, equity and inclusion.
questions.a: Sample: All three are about fairness, but they act at different points. Equality, in the left panel of Fig. 5.3, hands everyone the exact same support: three identical boxes, which leave the tallest comfortable and the shortest still unable to see, because identical treatment does not give identical benefit. Equity, in the right panel, shares the boxes out according to need, so all three can see over the fence; it takes account of existing inequalities and addresses them. Fig. 5.14 goes further and shows no boxes at all, because the fence itself is gone and everyone simply watches the match. That is inclusion: instead of distributing help so that people can cope with a barrier, it removes the barrier, which is why the chapter describes inclusion as removing barriers to participation. The progression matters because equity still marks out who needed the extra box, while inclusion changes the arrangement so that nobody needs one.
s: Explains equality as identical support that does not give identical benefit
Explains equity as support shared by need, addressing existing inequalities
Explains inclusion as removing the barrier itself, so extra support is no longer required

questions.q: Figure 5.15 is captioned 'Designing and creating facilities that are inclusive', and shows the same playground twice. Analyse what the two pictures together are saying.
questions.a: Sample: In the first picture the playground is perfectly ordinary and nobody in it is unkind: children run, swing and slide, and a child in a wheelchair sits at the edge watching them. He is excluded all the same, not by anything anyone said but by ground and equipment built without him in mind. In the second picture the same children are playing and he is among them, in the ball game, because the place itself has been made reachable. Together the two say that exclusion is often designed in rather than spoken, and that it can therefore be designed out. This is why the chapter says deliberate actions need to be taken to ensure inclusion: no amount of goodwill from the other children would have got the first playground to look like the second, and telling them to be kinder would have missed the cause entirely. It also explains the word creating in the caption -- a facility is inclusive when it is built that way, not when someone is later given help to manage it.
s: Describes the first picture as exclusion caused by the design of the place rather than by anyone's unkindness
Describes the second as the same place made reachable, so the child takes part
Draws the conclusion that exclusion can be designed in and designed out, requiring deliberate action rather than goodwill

questions.q: The chapter closes with the claim that 'Democracy is strengthened through enabling and facilitating participation of all.' Judge whether the chapter has made its case for this.
questions.a: Sample: I think it largely has, though the case is made by example rather than argument. The chapter's own definition of a citizen is someone who can participate in the decision-making of the country, so a democracy in which whole groups do not in fact take part is falling short of its own description, whatever the rules say. The examples support the claim well. The reading club shows that people who seem uninterested are often merely blocked, and that once the barrier goes the activity itself gets richer -- storytelling and puppetry arrived with the new members. The mock youth parliament, where students in remote areas joined the discussion through a voting app, makes the same point about the reach of participation. The weaker part of the case is that the chapter does not test the claim against any difficulty: it does not ask what to do when participation is costly or when people disagree sharply once included. But the central claim stands, because a democracy that hears from only some of its citizens is deciding on worse information than one that hears from all.
s: Connects the claim to the chapter's own definition of a citizen as one who participates in decision-making
Supports it with evidence from the chapter, such as the reading club or the mock youth parliament
Reaches a clear judgement and notes a limitation or counter-consideration

questions.q: Propose four steps your class could take to make itself more inclusive. Make each one a specific action rather than a good intention, and say which barrier it removes.
questions.a: Sample: One, rotate group membership by a drawn lot each time instead of letting friends pair off, which removes the barrier that leaves the same child picked last every time for reasons nobody admits. Two, agree that any class activity costing money is either funded from the class collection or is not held, which removes the barrier that kept Mina off the overnight trip and then had her judged for it. Three, put every notice and set of instructions in both English and the regional language, and read them aloud once, which removes the language barrier that kept students away from Smt. Amita's reading club and helps anyone who reads more slowly. Four, hold a one-minute pause before any group answer is finalised, in which the members who have not yet spoken are asked first, which removes the barrier faced by a classmate who takes longer to read or write and is otherwise talked over. All four are arrangements rather than appeals to be nicer, because the chapter says deliberate actions need to be taken to ensure inclusion.
s: Proposes a specific action addressing exclusion from groups, with the barrier named
Proposes a specific action addressing cost or economic background
Proposes a specific action addressing language or reading speed
Proposes a fourth specific action and shows these are arrangements rather than appeals to goodwill
